sorting-searching.summary: Know the properties of each sorting algorithm (time, space, stability, adaptivity), when non-comparison sorts beat n log n, and how to write binary search variants that always terminate and return the right boundary.
points: Merge sort is stable and always O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra space on arrays; quicksort is in place and usually fastest but degrades to O(n²) with bad pivots; heap sort is in place and O(n log n) but unstable.
Insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted input, and Python's Timsort detects sorted runs, so `sorted()` on presorted data makes only n − 1 comparisons.
Stable sorts let you sort by several keys: sort by the secondary key first, then by the primary key.
Comparison sorts need Ω(n log n) comparisons (⌈log₂ n!⌉); counting and radix sort avoid comparisons and run in O(n + k) or O(d(n + b)).

Binary search needs a range that strictly shrinks: if a branch sets `lo = mid`, use the upper middle `(lo + hi + 1) // 2`. `bisect_left` and `bisect_right` give the first and one-past-last positions of a value.
Binary search on the answer works whenever feasibility is monotonic (ship capacity, eating speed, kth value in a sorted matrix).
Quickselect finds the kth element in O(n) expected time; interval problems become linear scans after sorting by start.
traps: `lo = mid` with `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` loops forever on a two-element range.
Last-element (or first-element) pivots make quicksort quadratic on sorted input, and Lomuto partitioning is quadratic on all-equal input.
`bisect.insort` is O(n) per insert because list insertion shifts elements, even though the search is O(log n).
